meta.title: Rooms from a split footprint, with a circulation net
meta.description: THE SECOND CONSUMER of the subdivision `examples-facade` introduced, built to answer whether a `splitBounds` NODE is wanted. The answer it gives is no, and the reason is specific: the split machinery is identical between the two graphs -- the argmax over the three spans, the cut decided on the parent, the two-copy `repeatPoints` fan-out, the one `setBounds` that rewrites both corners from the box the cell arrived with -- and ONLY THE STOP RULE differs. A facade wants panels under a bounded SIZE; a plan wants rooms under a bounded floor AREA, because a long thin room has a small area while its longest wall says otherwise. A node would have to take the stop rule as a field to serve both, at which point it is `repeatUntil` with extra steps. What the two graphs share is a RECIPE WITH ONE HOLE IN IT, and extracting it into `src/primitives/` is the obvious move -- deliberately not made here. The hole is not what stops it: a primitive's param accepts a FIELD, spliced in where the body reads it and evaluated per element -- through a nested `repeatUntil` too, when the loop exposes the param and the primitive's declaration targets it -- so a recipe could take the stop rule whole, `gt(longest span, 1.7)` from the facade or `gt(area, 26)` from the plan. What two consumers do not settle is the recipe's shape around the hole: which of the cut range, the depth cap and the per-cell kind become knobs, and what it hands back. A third consumer is what would show that. A ROOM IS A POINT, exactly as a panel was: `boundsMin`/`boundsMax` is the room, and the plan is the set of leaves. The root box is thin in Y, so the vertical span is never the longest and every cut falls on one of the two floor axes, whichever is longer at that cell (which is not the same as alternating) -- the same trick the facade uses to stay flat, turned ninety degrees. THE KIND IS READ OFF THE AREA, which is the thing the facade deliberately did not have. A cell with no kind splits by one rule and makes a Mondrian; giving each leaf a STRING kind is what turns a subdivision into a plan you can talk about. It is spelled as `setAttribute` with an INDEX selector -- `ge(area, 13) + ge(area, 19)` counts how many thresholds an area clears and lands on 0, 1 or 2 in `values` -- because the grammar has no `and`/`or` and no switch, and summing predicates is how a staircase of thresholds is written here. THE BANDS MUST SIT INSIDE THE STOP RULE'S RANGE, which is not obvious and cost a cook: a cell stops splitting once its floor area is 26 or less (the literal in `stillOpen`), so a threshold ABOVE 26 can never fire and every room comes back the same kind. With a cut fraction in [0.34, 0.66), a child keeps at least 0.34 of a parent larger than 26, so the leaves land in roughly [0.34, 1] of that floor -- 8.9 to 26.0 square units over seeds 0 to 199 -- and the bands at 13 and 19 are chosen inside that. The depth cap of 9 that the facade's stop rule also carries never binds here: every seed from 0 to 199 has stopped on area by depth 7. That column is a real string attribute: `byAttribute` can dispatch on it, `filterByAttribute` can cut on it, and `spawnInstances` could send each kind to a different asset. DOORS ARE A PROXIMITY GRAPH, AND THAT IS NOT THE SAME AS ADJACENCY -- said plainly because the picture will not say it. `connectPoints` in `relativeNeighborhood` mode over the room centres keeps a pair only when no third centre is closer to both, which thins the complete graph into a circulation-looking net that still contains a spanning tree, so the plan is connected. But two rooms sharing a wall are not always each other's near neighbours, and two rooms that merely pass close diagonally can be joined. A true adjacency test asks whether two boxes share a FACE, which is a question about a pair of cells that no node in this library asks. Reading this graph as 'which rooms are next to each other' is reading it wrong; reading it as 'a circulation net over the rooms' is what it is. WHAT IT INHERITS WITHOUT RESTATING: the axis and the cut coordinate are decided on the PARENT, before `repeatPoints` fans it out, and every child reads them from the columns it carried -- because the two halves of a cell have different seeds (copy k gets hashCombine(seed, k)) and a cut drawn on each child would land at two different coordinates, leaving a strip that belongs to neither half or to both. The facade's description carries that measurement, invisible in the render; the same guard is why the rooms here tile their footprint exactly, 560 square units of leaves over a 560 square unit root.
